paras: The whipping of Bun near Fender, Georgia, was the reported flogging in late August 1903 of a 15-year-old Black youth accused of having been at a young white woman's bedside at night. Captured by local men who set out to take him to the jail at Tifton, he escaped before arriving, and rumor held that he had been severely flogged and told to leave the country.
Bun was employed on the place near Fender where Mrs. Bradshaw, described as a young white woman, lived.

According to a Tifton dispatch dated August 27, Mrs. Bradshaw awoke during the previous night to find a Black youth at her bedside, raised the alarm, and recognized him "despite the dim light" as Bun. The men who answered her call chased him so closely that he fled without his clothes, and during the night he took an old pair of trousers from an outhouse. The next morning he was tracked and captured at about 11 o'clock.

Several young men then started with him toward the Tifton jail, but he escaped before they reached it. The dispatch added that "Rumor says" he got away with "one of the most thorough floggings that a boy of his size ever received" and was warned "to leave the country and stay away."
No report of an arrest, charge or inquiry concerning either the alleged entry or the flogging appears in the coverage, and no account from Bun himself was found.

The episode is known from a single Tifton dispatch printed on page 2 of the Savannah Morning News on August 28, 1903. Its headline, "WHIPPED A NEGRO," stated the whipping as fact, while the body attributed it only to rumor, and its subhead, "Woman's Screams Had Put Him to Flight," foregrounded the woman's account. The story repeated Mrs. Bradshaw's version without qualification and named neither the pursuers nor any motive beyond her alarm.
No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press or in other white papers.
